name: Facet
text: To achieve our goal of owning the visual presentation of the interface, I propose we prioritize a dark mode design for our application. This decision will enhance visibility and clarity, especially for users who work in low-light environments, and it's a popular preference among many users. By choosing dark mode as our primary design, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially increased complexity in designing compatible color schemes and typography. This trade-off is worth it, as a well-designed dark mode will significantly contribute to the overall enjoyment and liveliness of our interface.

name: Pane
text: Pane: Hold on—dark mode’s a fine *preference*, but it’s not a *risk-free* choice. What about users who toggle between light and dark modes unpredictably, or those with visual impairments who rely on high-contrast light interfaces? A better alternative might be a *system-preference-first* approach: default to the OS setting, then let users override it. That way, we avoid forcing a one-size-fits-all solution and actually respect user agency. Settle it by testing both in a small cohort—track completion rates and satisfaction, not just aesthetics.

name: Facet
text:
I understand Pane's concerns about dark mode, but I still think we should implement a system-preference-first approach, where our application defaults to the user's system-wide theme preference, whether it's light or dark mode. This decision allows us to cater to the majority of users who have already chosen their preferred theme, while also considering users with visual impairments who rely on high-contrast interfaces. By doing so, we're accepting the trade-off of added complexity in maintaining multiple theme options, but I believe it's worth it to provide a more inclusive and user-friendly experience. This approach will ultimately enhance the overall clarity and enjoyment of our interface, aligning with our goal of owning the visual presentation.

name: Pane
text: Pane: Wait—defaulting to system preference isn’t risk-free either. What about users who *never* set their system theme, leaving it on some forgotten default that clashes with our interface? Or those who switch themes mid-session for accessibility reasons, only to have our app fight them? A better alternative is *user-choice-first*: let the user pick once, store it, and respect it—no guessing, no fights with their OS. That settles it: build a persistent toggle, log the decision, and move on.
